column3: The Hebrew says “all his people”; BSB interprets this as “his whole army.”
“The Amorite” is a collective singular in Hebrew; BSB uses plural “the Amorites.”
The Hebrew has singular “our hand,” “all his people,” and “we struck him,” and says that no survivor was left “to him.” BSB uses “hands,” “army,” and “them,” and omits the final recipient.
The Hebrew says there was no city we did not take “from them”; BSB leaves that phrase implicit.
“Wall” and “bar” are singular in Hebrew; BSB uses plurals and calls the open cities “villages.”
The Hebrew repeats the same root for devoting to destruction; BSB varies it with “utterly destroying.”
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew retains the image “from the hand of two kings” and uses collective singular “the Amorite.” It calls Arnon a stream or wadi rather than a valley.
The Hebrew repeats the name Hermon and uses collective singular “the Amorite.”
The Hebrew concludes “cities of the kingdom of Og in Bashan”; BSB connects “cities” directly with Salecah and Edrei and omits the final Bashan.
The Hebrew repeats “bed,” asks rhetorically whether it is in Rabbah, and specifies a man’s cubit. BSB makes the location a statement with “still” and omits the final specification.
The Hebrew starts the allotment “from Aroer,” rather than “beyond Aroer,” and uses collective singular names for the Reubenite and Gadite.
The designation “is called” is expressed as a general description in Hebrew; BSB has “used to be called.”
The Hebrew calls Jair “son of Manasseh,” uses collective singulars for the Geshurite and Maacathite, and says “called,” rather than “renamed.”
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew uses collective singular names for the Reubenite and Gadite and calls Arnon a stream or wadi. “Sons of Ammon” becomes “Ammonites.”
The Hebrew lists the Arabah and Jordan and says “under the slopes of Pisgah”; BSB reshapes the list into a border description.
The Hebrew says “sons of Israel” and “all sons of strength”; BSB has “Israelites” and “all your men of valor.”
The Hebrew explicitly says “your cities”; BSB leaves that possessive implicit.
Close to the Hebrew.
Close to the Hebrew.
The Hebrew describes the LORD as the one fighting for you; BSB uses the future “will fight.”
The Hebrew has “and” and “saying”; BSB supplies “also.”
The Hebrew retains the image “Your strong hand” and links heaven and earth with “and”; BSB has “power” and “or.”
The Hebrew repeats “good” for the land and hill country; BSB varies this as “good” and “pleasant.”
The Hebrew reports that He did not listen, without explicitly saying He would not.
The Hebrew says “lift up your eyes” and then “see with your eyes”; BSB condenses the first image and supplies “the land.”
The Hebrew explicitly says “this people”; BSB has “the people.”
Close to the Hebrew.
